doc.title: Paul Shaffer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 24, 2023

title: Gigs with the band: school dances, the hockey arena and union scale
summary: Music gave him a social place in high school; he describes dances and Saturday gigs at the Fort William Gardens, $24 scale, and joining the union through Rocky Albertini.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: I was going to ask if you negotiated the sometimes intense social atmosphere in high school because you had this persona. You weren’t a jock or you weren’t, I don’t know you might have been a straight A student, but you had the music thing. Did that help you?
Sure. I guess certainly it did, thinking back to high school days and stuff. But being in a band as it were wasn’t quite the same up in Fort William, Ontario.
Describe a gig for me up there.

Well the gigs we were playing I was 15 going into 16 and stayed in this band until I graduated and left town to go to college. So a gig, you know we would play the school dances. That’s really what we did, and then we had a regular Saturday night gig at the Fort William Gardens, a hockey arena where they would put plywood down on the ice and erect a stage and that’s what we would play on a stage of about I don’t know you know six feet high. Six, seven feet high up. A hockey arena. Booming sound. No such thing as stage monitors at that time. No such thing as roadies, that’s the main thing. Because at the end of the gig, you know, and I had my own amplifier and small combo © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-
organ and I would be loading it into my parents’ car at the end of the night and it wasn’t so glamorous as all of that.
Do you remember what kind of bread were you making on the average hockey rink gig?
24 dollars perhaps a night. That was scale. Rocky Albertini specified.
Oh so it was actually a union —

Yes sir. That’s why I had to join. I guess that’s what sparked me thinking about Ricky Lazar you know. I joined his band, it was a union band. I had to join the union right away. Go down and see Rocky Albertini in the back of his shoe store, and he signed me up and I had to promise him, you know, “Don’t be giving away too many of those appearances in the assemblies. I want to know about them when they ask you to play at the school, I want to be able to okay them or not.” So I had to call Rocky Albertini, yes indeed. And then eventually both of us forgot about it. But yes that’s how I started out, absolutely a union man which I have been all these years. And that was the scale.
